newsitem.title: USA: House OKs nutrition aid increase on spending bill.
newsitem.headline: House OKs nutrition aid increase on spending bill.

text.p: The House Thursday voted to increase funding for a special nutrition programme for the poor, for pregnant women and for children, as it debated a bill to provide $5.5 billion in disaster aid to weather-ravaged states.
By a vote of 338-89, the House agreed to the full $76 million requested by the White House for the Women, Infants and Children programme, which povides vouchers for food and baby formula.
Republican leaders originally included only half that amount in the bill. The White House said nearly 200,000 poor children would lose benefits unless the House provided the additional $38 million.

"This should not be a partisan issue. This is about funding poor children who need food in their mouths ... this is about taking food out of the mouths of little babies," said New Jersey Republican Representative Marge Roukema, a sponsor of the bipartisan amendment.
But some Republicans charged Democrats and the states had played politics with the issue, saying there was more than enough money in the pipeline to support those now in the programme.

"The ugliness of demagoguery and grandstanding have crept into the WIC programme this year," New Mexico Republican Joe Skeen said. "In a very concerted political move to show who loves children, we have have state WIC directors telling misleading stories."
The House hoped to complete work later Thursday on the spending measure, which would aid more than 30 states devastated by floods and other natural disasters.
The measure also included nearly $2 billion to fund U.S. peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and U.S. military flights in the Gulf.

Congressional leaders had hoped to move the bill quickly through Congress. It instead became the forum for a pitched battle over policy issues ranging from printing U.S. currency to nutrition aid for the poor.
House Republican leaders were embarrassed Wednesday when 43 members of their party revolted and helped defeat a rule needed to bring the measure to the floor.

To satisfy critics, Republicans agreed to allow a separate vote on the WIC funding, drop an amendment that would have cut off funding for U.S. peacekeeping operations in Bosnia after June 30, 1998, and make other changes.

The biggest point of contention remaining was an amendment that would automatically continue funding if Congress failed to enact final spending bills. Clinton threatened to veto the bill if the amendment was included.
Budget disputes forced two unpopular government shutdowns in fiscal 1996, which the public blamed on Republicans.
